summary:
Niger is among the most dangerous countries in the region for a trans visitor, and the legal position hardened sharply in 2025 and 2026. In March 2025 the ruling junta's Charter of Refoundation banned “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” in Article 25, the first explicit statutory-level outlawing of same-sex conduct in the country's history. The ban operates alongside the five-year transition declared after the July 2023 coup.

The prohibition is now carried in the penal code. A February 2026 revision of the penal code criminalises “indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts” under article 390, punishable by five to ten years' imprisonment and fines; same-sex marriage under article 391 carries ten to twenty years; article 392 targets LGBTQIA+ associations. Article 390 also reaches anyone who “artificially changes sex at birth”, a clause that on its face exposes trans and intersex people to imprisonment for transition-related procedures. The state news agency confirmed on 1 June 2026 that LGBTQIA+ practice is criminalised under the 2026 revision.

The drafting is broad enough that reporting on the law reads asexuality as among the sanctionable conducts, so the exposure is not confined to sexual acts between people of the same sex. An earlier 2023 draft penal code, which did not take effect in that form, proposed up to five years for same-sex conduct, twenty years for conducting, officiating or witnessing a same-sex marriage, and five years for participating in or financing “homosexual” organisations; it also fixed age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts against 13 for different-sex acts, a distinction that would expose adult same-sex partners to prosecution.

Enforcement under junta rule has been immediate and public. By 1 July 2026 at least 40 people had been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, were imprisoned following the new penal code. Campaigners describe a witch-hunt atmosphere. Arrest under these provisions carries the risk of outing anyone travelling with a partner or documented history, and detention by security forces under a military government offers no meaningful avenue of complaint.

Earlier precedent points the same way. In 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency article 276, which carries up to three years; the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them, showing the cost of delivering an acquittal. In December 2022 the national legislature backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, weeks after a subnational court had acquitted two young women precisely because no statute criminalised same-sex conduct.

Access to HIV prevention has deteriorated alongside criminalisation: sources report that PrEP drug access has collapsed, with campaigners warning of an AIDS resurgence among men who have sex with men. No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, document markers, entry screening, or facilities access; those must be treated as unassessed rather than safe.
tangentialFactors:
Niger's 2025–2026 measures sit within a wider pattern of states across the continent hardening anti-LGBTQIA+ statutes, so the country is not an isolated case in the region and visitors crossing borders should expect comparable or worse exposure in neighbouring jurisdictions.

The security context compounds the legal risk: rule by a military junta since the July 2023 coup means the enforcement apparatus is a military one, and the imprissonment of senior military officials for homosexuality indicates that the campaign reaches into institutions that would ordinarily be considered insulated.

Campaigners' framing of a witch-hunt and the reported collapse of PrEP supply suggest the surrounding public-health and social climate is deteriorating, which raises the risk of community violence and denunciation independent of formal charges.
localsOnly:
Residents face the full weight of the 2026 penal code: article 390 (five to ten years plus fines) for indecent, unnatural and LGBTQIA+ acts, article 391 (ten to twenty years) for same-sex marriage, and article 392 against LGBTQIA+ associations, effectively barring organised advocacy.

Article 390's prohibition on “artificially chang[ing] sex at birth” and the intersex rights criticism of the law mean that transition-related and bodily autonomy procedures are themselves sanctionable conduct for residents, not merely identity expression.

Residents also face the age-of-consent differential carried in the draft provisions, 21 for same-sex acts against 13 for different-sex acts, and the earlier use of public-indecency article 276 (up to three years) to prosecute alleged same-sex intimacy where no specific statute applied.

Judicial independence is a practical constraint: the trial judge who acquitted two women in 2023 was reassigned to an administrative post, so acquittals have carried professional punishment for the judge.

Residents living with HIV face a narrowing care pathway, with PrEP access reported as collapsing and campaigners warning of an AIDS resurgence.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in the inventory states whether the 2023 draft penal code's specific penalties took independent effect or were wholly absorbed into the February 2026 revision; the two sets of figures (five years, twenty years, five years in the draft versus 5–10, 10–20 in the 2026 code) may describe the same instruments or different ones.

Unresolved: the claim that asexuality falls within the sanctionable conduct rests on a single newspaper reading of the drafting, not on judicial interpretation or official comment; no court ruling applying article 390 to asexual or aromantic persons is sourced here.

Unresolved: the Charter of Refoundation's Article 25 is reported as setting no specific penalties itself, and the relationship between charter provisions and penal code articles in enforcement practice is not documented in the inventory.

Not sourced in this inventory: legal gender recognition and document-marker rules, entry and visa screening procedures that could expose a trans traveller's status, public facilities or bathroom restrictions, and any hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection. Silence in these sources should not be read as a permissive position.

Unresolved: the exact status of the 40 arrests and 16 imprisonments reported on 1 July 2026, including charges, convictions and sentences, is not detailed beyond the campaigner account.
